doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Making his way in New York
title: Professionals Unlimited, the bass players' organization
summary: He describes a clique of bass players from different cities who joined to promote the bass violin. He was no threat because he had no clique of his own.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So then you started getting calls, maybe to sub for people? “Hey I can’t make my gig tonight, can you cover for me?” Is that how that works?

Yeah. I was telling you downstairs about the organization. And so this puts it in — this is going to make history now, but it was a group called Professionals Unlimited. And basically they didn’t think that we — basically it was an organized clique. But what makes it remarkable out of all kinds of cliques was that these were all bass players from different cities. See at the time there was a Chicago clique, there was a Detroit clique,

you know, there was a Los Angeles clique there was a Bos — so what I mean by that is usually those groups exchanged work among themselves. But what happened when all of these bass players came together with a common purpose, in other words to dramatize the bass violin — “Wow, we’ve got a little stew here.” The guy from Detroit, we’re at a meeting, “Hey I’ve got this” — but what my forte was, was that where I came from they didn’t really have a clique. So I wasn’t a threat to anyone. I just had to play good. And that’s what I tried to do every time I put out. I played with all my heart and soul. That’s what happened.
